title: US soft-water lakes lost sulfate but not calcium in 2007-2022, so lower acid deposition did not start the calcium path to fewer Daphnia; Holopedium and Daphnia follow calcium between lakes
abstract: Question: in US lakes, did the decrease of sulfur deposition cause the calcium (Ca) decrease that harms Daphnia and helps the jelly-coated Holopedium, as found in Canadian Shield lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008, 2015)? Data: US EPA National Lakes Assessment 2007, 2012, 2017 and 2022 (914 lakes sampled in two or more cycles, 1,150 revisit pairs), coarse-net zooplankton counts, EPA/NADP TDep sulfur deposition (5-year means) and NOAA nClimDiv climate. The analysis plan was written before outcome models were fitted. Results: median modelled S deposition at the lakes fell from 3.9 to 1.6 kg/ha/yr. In 243 soft-water revisit pairs (first-visit Ca < 5 mg/L), lake sulfate fell 17% per 5 years (change of log -0.186, 95% CI -0.253 to -0.119), more where initial deposition was high. Ca did not fall (+0.026 per 5 years, -0.007 to +0.059), also not at Ca < 2 mg/L, in eastern soft lakes, or in lakes without chloride gain. Base cations did not follow sulfate (F = 0.40, -0.39 to +1.19) but followed chloride. The biological relation exists in space: Holopedium was present in 56% of lakes with Ca < 1.5 mg/L and 1% above 20 mg/L; Daphnia in 57% and 71-77%; with controls, log Ca had a positive Daphnia-share term (+0.65 in lakes with Ca < 10 mg/L) and a negative Holopedium term (-0.79). Within lakes (2012-2022), Ca gain came with Holopedium loss (presence -0.22 per log Ca at Ca < 10 mg/L), but Daphnia slopes were uncertain in soft lakes and the hard-lake negative control failed. Exploratory: Daphnia presence fell 12 points in the same lakes in 2017-2022, mostly where it was rare, at the same time as a much smaller 2022 large-and-rare scan; Ca did not explain it. Conclusion: lower deposition reached lake sulfate but not lake Ca in 2007-2022, so the jellification path was not active on average in the US national sample. Limitations: one visit per cycle, few very soft lakes, modelled deposition, unweighted revisit subset, laboratory and protocol changes between cycles, and no data before 2007.

citations.reason: Jeziorski et al. 2008: widespread Ca decline after acid deposition decrease and Daphnia Ca thresholds. We test the chain in US lakes; the Ca decrease did not occur in 2007-2022.
Jeziorski et al. 2015: jellification (Holopedium rise) with Ca decline. Our space results support the Holopedium-Ca relation.
